rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without a Day of Judgment, good and evil would be treated alike and creation would be purposeless; 68:35–36 makes the same objection to denying accountability.
rows.anchor: are We to treat alike the obedient and the criminals?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daylight and night sustain material life, while ease and hardship train the moral and spiritual self in gratitude and patience, preparing people for the state described in 89:28.
rows.anchor: they will be happy with their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of night and day shows that every created thing is governed by God, so even powerful people cannot escape His control.
rows.anchor: It is He who releases and restrains it and it is He who sets it free.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath's signs of release and restraint emphasize God's control, as illustrated by the possibility of perpetual night or day in 28:71–72.
rows.anchor: no one, however much powerful he may be, should arrogantly reckon that he is beyond His control.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥijr means intellect; both words carry the sense of restraining or tying up, and intellect is an inner leash against undignified conduct.
rows.anchor: Both contain the meaning of “stopping and tying up.” In other words, intellect is an inner leash

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative rebukes while decisively asserting that a sensible person should learn from nearby signs instead of waiting to see the Hereafter before believing.
rows.anchor: when he is able to sight his destination.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After earlier signs failed to convince the stubborn, the most manifest and nearby signs are presented as testimony for the sensible, though the stubborn will not benefit.
rows.anchor: those signs have been presented before them which are the most manifest and near them and contain a testimony within them for the sensible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse turns from signs in nature to history, which also testifies that God observes nations and holds them accountable.
rows.anchor: After pointing out the signs present in the world around man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants nations a wise respite to mend their ways, then seizes them; their destruction anticipates accountability for every person, with full reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: the whole world also will be held accountable one day in which each and every individual will be held responsible for his deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ād are linked to Iram, described as an ancestral line beginning with Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ.
rows.anchor: The Iram are from among their forefathers from whom began great feats

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “Iram of the pillars” is associated with the Ād's construction achievements; the author compares this symbolic usage with the cauldrons and basins associated with Solomon in 34:13.
rows.anchor: symbolically refer to the generosity of Solomon (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ād excelled at stone carving and built monuments on high places; Hūd criticized this wasteful, boastful pursuit, and they were exceptionally strong.
rows.anchor: They had carved beautiful pavilions and castles from mountains.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamūd descended from the Ād, inherited their building arts, were also called the second Ād, and carved mountain homes in Wād al-Qurā.
rows.anchor: They had carved houses from the mountains of this valley

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pharaoh of the pegs” refers symbolically to his army, whose tents were secured with pegs; Arabic commonly uses this image for armies.
rows.anchor: For this distinctive feature, the Pharaoh is called “of the pegs.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the usual temporary forces assembled by families and tribes, Pharaoh maintained a standing army; the Torah also describes its size, and nobles had to keep horses, weapons, and chariots.
rows.anchor: once the need was fulfilled, they would go back to their work.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nations' rebellion meant indifference and fearlessness toward God, coupled with the conceit that their status and resources were self-earned and beyond accountability.
rows.anchor: These people were rebellious in their lands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pride and conceit led these peoples away from the right path, under Satan and base desires, until evil spread in individual and collective life.
rows.anchor: As a result, evil spread in their individual and collective lives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's punishment followed when the evil these nations spread had pervaded every sphere of their lives.
rows.anchor: the Almighty as a result unleashed His punishment on them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice is to monitor nations entrusted with political power, allow time for reform or a final communication of truth, and destroy persistently rebellious nations; even those at their zenith cannot avert it.
rows.anchor: He continues to watch over it and sees if it is properly using this authority.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 14 summarizes the opening oaths and historical examples and functions as the oath's asserted conclusion, supported by natural signs and history.
rows.anchor: This is the summary of all the oaths and historical anecdotes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirsād means an ambush site: God watches everything, grants only limited respite, then seizes rebellious nations when their term ends.
rows.anchor: the place where one lies in ambush

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's active governance and the rise and fall of nations show that creation has purpose and entail a coming Judgment with reward for obedience and punishment for disorder.
rows.anchor: there is a Day of Judgement which will necessarily come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People wrongly treat worldly abundance as proof of divine esteem and hardship as proof of humiliation; both conditions are tests, not judgments of worth.
rows.anchor: The consequence of this misconception is that the first category of people is overcome by conceit and vanity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affluence tests gratitude, obedience, and care for others; hardship tests contentment and resolve. Strength in both forms of trial strengthens faith and yields a peaceful soul.
rows.anchor: If the Almighty blesses someone with affluence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affluent leaders of Makkah and Ṭā’if are reproached: wealth is a test calling for gratitude and service to orphans and the poor, but instead made them proud and contemptuous.
rows.anchor: the affluent leaders of Makkah and Ṭā’if are addressed directly and admonished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kindness to orphans requires a respected social status and protection from hardship, not merely spending; wealth has value before God when used for their welfare.
rows.anchor: Orphans should not be left at the mercy of adverse circumstances; people should honour and respect them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for urging means exhorting one another; society should actively encourage orphan welfare rather than conceal stinginess, and “food” broadly means meeting all their needs.
rows.anchor: The objective is to cater for all their needs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their greed led powerful members of society to seize inheritance and deprive weak heirs, even children, of their shares.
rows.anchor: The implication is that they have become so infatuated with the love of wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In jāhiliyyah, influential people used a self-made rule that the strongest heir took a deceased person's wealth, leaving the weak with no share, despite Islam's prohibition of misappropriation.
rows.anchor: the person who was the most powerful would have the right on the wealth left by a deceased; the weak had no share in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obsessive love of wealth blinds people to humanitarianism, decency, justice, and compassion, leaving higher values no place in their hearts.
rows.anchor: The lust for wealth has made them blind to everything else and made them indifferent to the values of humanitarianism, decency, justice and compassion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those enamored of wealth will recognize their folly and wish they had prepared for the Day, but that regret will be useless when they face the consequences of their deeds.
rows.anchor: all this would prove fruitless for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kallā” rejects the notion that wealth proves divine honor: the earth will be leveled and worldly life will end; 18:7–8 presents the same testing purpose and barren-earth outcome.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has bestowed honour on him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's adornments are temporary; they test whether people prepare for the next world or immerse themselves in worldly pursuits, before landforms and buildings are destroyed and leveled.
rows.anchor: all these embellishments of the earth will be no more.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tests humanity while unseen but will reveal Himself with the angels at Judgment, when reality is so clear that no doubt remains.
rows.anchor: the reality will stare people in their eyes in such a blatant manner that no one will be left with any doubt about it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The details of how God appears concern mutashābihāt; believers should affirm them broadly rather than pursue specifics and risk straying.
rows.anchor: If a person starts to go after their details, there is a strong chance of him going astray.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise and Hell will also be unveiled, with Hell mentioned first because the sūrah's principal addressees are Islam's active adversaries; seeing it will bring them despair.
rows.anchor: Since the real addressees of this sūrah are the proactive adversaries of Islam, Hell is mentioned first.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 24 explains the person's realization in verse 23: those who now dismiss warnings will regret failing to prepare for the Hereafter, but the time to amend will have passed.
rows.anchor: The time to make amends for it would be long gone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse states the severity of divine punishment: unlike earthly suffering, which death can end, punishment and confinement in the Hereafter cannot be escaped through death.
rows.anchor: in the Hereafter even death will not be able to save a person from the punishment and incarceration he would have to face.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The peaceful soul is the opposite of those who respond to ease with pride and hardship with despair; it stays true in both, gives thanks and helps others in ease, and perseveres in adversity.
rows.anchor: If they are blessed with favours, they think that they are being tested whether they show gratitude to the Almighty or not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those content with God through comfort and adversity are called contented souls and will dwell in Paradise.
rows.anchor: These are the people who will dwell in Paradise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's address praises those who passed their worldly trial and remained pleased with Him in every circumstance; their Lord is pleased with them in return.
rows.anchor: they are pleased with Him and He is pleased with them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having succeeded in their trial and become worthy of Paradise, the contented souls are invited to join God's servants close to Him and enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: since they have become worthy of Paradise after succeeding in their trial, they should now join His near ones in Paradise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Balad pairs with al-Fajr: both correct the view that ease proves honor and hardship humiliation, teaching gratitude and generosity in ease and patience in hardship; this yields the contented soul of 89:28.
rows.anchor: A person who adopts this attitude is a person whose soul is at peace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Balad applies this teaching to Quraysh: Makkah was once barren and insecure, then became prosperous and safe after Abraham's prayer for Ishmael and his descendants.
rows.anchor: it was also devoid of peace and security.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham prayed for provision and security for Ishmael's family; the land received both, allowing his descendants to multiply and gain leadership.
rows.anchor: the land not only became abundant with these resources

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After receiving these favors, Quraysh forgot their history, treated prosperity as a birthright, and balked at spending in God's way.
rows.anchor: these people forgot their previous history

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh's wealth is spent on amusement and waste; they praise God, persevere, and show kindness rarely, and lack resolve to sacrifice for the needy, thus heading toward Hell.
rows.anchor: All of them are treading the path that leads to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the sūrah is early Makkan, its address is generally “O man” and appeals to shared humanitarian values and natural moral norms.
rows.anchor: the appeal found in them is upon humanitarian grounds and upon its natural norms.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–4 cite Makkah's early barren history and the Ishmaelites' hardship, then God's favor, Abraham's prayer, and the House's blessing as causes of security and abundant provision.
rows.anchor: Testimony is presented from the early history of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5–7 rebuke people who claim they have spent a fortune: they should have thanked God and aided the needy, but think He does not see their wasteful spending.
rows.anchor: As an obligation towards these favours and blessings of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 8–17 list eyes, speech, moral awareness, freeing slaves, feeding the poor, faith, patience, and compassion as capacities and deeds that should overcome greed and serve God.
rows.anchor: the Almighty had given them eyes so that they could use them to learn the lessons of life, tongue and lips so that they could use them to urge people in helping the poor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 18–20 promise reward to those who choose the right path, while deniers of God's revelations earn Hell.
rows.anchor: If these people had adopted the right path, they would have been entitled to great reward in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed “lā” negates Quraysh's false inference that wealth means God honors them, a notion raised in al-Fajr; it dismisses the absurd claim before the oath without argument.
rows.anchor: No! I swear by this city

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by Makkah witnesses the claim in 90:4 that humans were created in hardship; like the Qur'anic oath in 95:3, it is evidence rather than an oath based on sacred status.
rows.anchor: No! I swear by this city

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 2 is parenthetical and intensifies the oath; its pronoun can address either the Prophet or Quraysh, since both know Makkah's history and current conditions firsthand.
rows.anchor: The implication is that it is not that the testimony of a far-flung area is being presented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father is Abraham, and his progeny is Ishmael's line, which first settled Makkah and later spread through Arabia.
rows.anchor: obviously refers to Abraham (sws) and Ishmael (sws)
